text.p: Britain's Duchess of York, who has called herself a disgrace, admitted on Thursday she had been "foolish and stupid" but denied having confessed to adultery and said all she wants is to be remembered as a good mother.

The former Sarah Ferguson, divorced last May from Queen Elizabeth's second son Prince Andrew, told an interviewer her lowest point had been press pictures showing her cavorting by a swimming pool with her Texan "financial adviser" John Bryan in 1992.
The 27-year-old duchess, better known as "Fergie", denied media reports that she had considered suicide. It was "purely faith that got me through that", she said on BBC radio.
Fergie, who is deeply in debt, is conducting a series of interviews to publicise her book "My Story".

Not all the publicity has been favourable. British tabloid newspapers highlighted the fact that an American interviewer had induced the duchess to deny that her long-suffering former husband was homosexual.
"Oh right, yeah, I really love that. There is absolutely no chance he can be gay," the duchess said." A lot of people believe it's true and it is categorically not true."
Her 10-year marriage to Prince Andrew was dogged by reports of her adultery. But the duchess refused to be drawn into confirming she had been unfaithful to her sailor husband.
"Have I admitted that? Where did I admit that? I haven't admitted it," the duchess said. "There are very firmly two sides to every story."
Pressed further on whether she had been unfaithful, the normally outspoken Fergie said: "I don't think that's relevant to this interview."
She added: "I think you can be very lonely and isolated and incredibly vulnerable, and very open to a small amount of kindness shown."

Fergie seemed happier to discuss free-spending habits which had swelled her debts to seven figures and to stress that she had "taken responsibility" for them and would pay them back as soon as she could.
"I am now over that and have taken control of my life," the duchess said. "I am standing here for truth."

Looking back over a career that inflicted severe damage on the monarchy -- apart from the adultery scandals and the debts, she has been criticised for everything from her dress sense and weight to her penchant for holidays abroad -- the duchess admitted she had not always been happy.
"I was the classic example of self-hatred," she said. "The book was like a therapy session for me."

In the book, the duchess blames Buckingham Palace courtiers -- whom she calls the "grey men of the Firm" -- and the British secret service of sabotaging her. She said they wanted to warn Princess Diana, then married to Andrew's brother Charles, the heir to the throne, that the same could happen to her if she did not behave.
The duchess said she had always been "very honest" with her two children, Beatrice, seven, and Eugenie, six, about what was going on, so they could see that "we all make mistakes".
She added: "The only thing I can probably say that I am good at is being a mother."
